In the 1860s, construction workers demolished a row of adjacent brick tombs to bring light into neighboring basements, resulting in the permanent disappearance of Declaration of Independence signer John Hancock's remains.

It was originally called the South or Common Burying Ground and was renamed in 1737 after a granary building that stood where Park Street Church is today. The cemetery contains about 2,345 gravestones but is estimated to hold over 5,000 burials, including many notable Revolutionary War figures such as John Hancock, Samuel Adams, Paul Revere, and victims of the Boston Massacre. The original layout of the gravestones was rearranged in the 19th century into neat rows to accommodate lawn mowing, a modern innovation at the time. Underground family crypts line the perimeter of the site, with older tombs located in the center. The burying ground was once part of Boston Common, and livestock grazing there helped maintain the landscaping before modern groundskeeping methods were introduced.

The congregation of Boston's Third Church commissioned master builder Joshua Blanchard to construct the brick meeting house in 1729 to replace an outgrown 1669 wooden building. 

Because it was the largest indoor space in colonial Boston, town leaders routinely chose it over Faneuil Hall to hold mass protest assemblies, including the five-thousand-person gathering on December 16, 1773, that directly launched the Boston Tea Party. 

During the British siege of Boston in 1775, occupying troops retaliated by ripping out its pews and pulpit, dumping dirt across the floor, and converting the sanctuary into a riding school for British cavalry. 

The congregation had to spend eight years raising funds after the occupation simply to repair the interior and restore it to religious use. 

In 1876, the congregation sold the building for demolition and materials after moving to Copley Square, prompting twenty Boston women to organize a public campaign that bought it back for $400,000 to halt its destruction.

The building was saved from demolition in 1876 by a group of twenty Boston women and has operated as a museum since 1877. The clock on its tower was made by Gawen Brown and installed in 1770. Notable members of its congregation included African-American poet Phillis Wheatley and patriots such as Samuel Adams and William Dawes. serper.text: Cours Saleya is located in the old town of Nice and is known for its daily flower market, which runs from Tuesday to Sunday mornings year-round. The name "Cours Saleya" likely derives from either "Sale" meaning salt or "Sole" meaning sun, reflecting the area's historical connection to salt storage and its sunny climate. In 1897, Nice opened the first wholesale cut flower market in the world at Cours Saleya, where growers from nearby hills brought flowers daily for bulk purchase before the market opened to individuals. The flower market was historically significant enough that flowers were shipped by rail from Nice to cities across France and Europe for nearly 100 years. On Mondays, the market transforms into an antique market, while in summer evenings, an artisan market selling souvenirs and crafts takes place. The market also sells local specialties such as socca, a chickpea flour pancake, which is baked nearby and brought to the market daily.

Bishop Didier Palletis commissioned the construction of the cathedral in the mid-17th century after the earlier medieval parish church on the site was judged too small for the growing town. 

Architect Jean-André Guibert modeled the structure on the church of Santa Susanna in Rome. 

The cathedral was dedicated to Saint Reparata to house relics that had arrived in Nice in 1060, following the local legend that angels guided a boat carrying the martyred teenager across the sea to the city's bay. 

Construction faced significant delays, spanning from 1650 to its consecration in 1699, with the bell tower left unbuilt until the mid-18th century and its current facade postponed until around 1830. 

Individual local trade corporations and aristocratic families had to fund and maintain the ten interior chapels themselves.

By 1590, the church of St Reparata was officially recognized as a cathedral after the seat of the bishops of Nice was transferred from Cimiez Cathedral. Bishop Didier Palletis commissioned the architect Jean-André Guibert in 1649 to build a larger cathedral, leading to the construction of the current main building between 1650 and 1685. The square did not exist in its modern form during the Middle Ages, as the area directly in front of Sainte-Réparate Cathedral was formerly choked by dense residential buildings and narrow alleyways. 

Local dignitary Charles Rossetti de Châteauneuf bequeathed his properties and land opposite the cathedral to the city of Nice so the church could have an open forecourt. 

His bequest enabled the municipality to demolish the obstructing apartment buildings in 1825 to clear and widen the open public space. 

The city named the newly created square in honor of the Rossetti family to recognize their civic philanthropy.

gemini.text:
The palace was commissioned in the mid-17th century by the aristocratic Lascaris-Vintimille family, nephews of Jean-Paul de Lascaris-Castellar, the 57th Grand Master of the Knights of Malta. 

The family lost ownership of the residence during the turmoil following the French Revolution and sold it in 1802. 

Over the subsequent decades, the former noble mansion deteriorated significantly as the surrounding neighborhood decayed into an impoverished quarter divided into tenement housing. 

To prevent further degradation and demolition, the City of Nice purchased the damaged structure in 1942. 

Squatters continued to occupy parts of the building until major municipal restoration work finally commenced in 1962. 

The site reopened in 1970 and later became a municipal music museum following the 1901 bequest of over two hundred historical musical instruments by Nice resident Antoine Gautier.

The city of Nice purchased the palace in 1942 with the intention of creating a museum. After restorations from 1962 to 1970, the building was opened to the public as a museum showcasing Baroque art and culture. The museum’s collection of over 500 historical musical instruments is largely based on the bequest of Antoine Gautier, a 19th-century Niçois amateur musician and collector. The Palais Lascaris is recognized as the most remarkable monument of Nice’s civil Baroque style and is listed as a historic monument since 1946. Guided tours are available by reservation, providing visitors with insights into the palace’s aristocratic history and its musical instrument collection.

The fortified citadel atop the hill was built starting in the medieval period to protect the town and serve as a strategic military stronghold.

During the 1705–1706 siege, French artillery fire breached the fortress when a bomb struck its munitions depot, causing a catastrophic explosion that cost hundreds of defenders their lives.

Following the fortress's capture, King Louis XIV ordered the complete demolition of the citadel, ramparts, and cathedral so that no defensive bastion remained to resist French rule.

King Charles Felix of Sardinia decided in 1822 to grant the barren military lands to the city of Nice to develop public promenades and gardens for locals and winter visitors.

The elevator shaft carrying visitors up through the hill was originally excavated as a deep water well to supply the military garrison.

serper.text: The Colline du Château in Nice was originally a military citadel built from the 11th century and stood until the 18th century before being destroyed by order of Louis XIV in 1706. The castle was besieged multiple times, notably in 1543 and 1691, before French troops took it in 1705. The hill was a strategic trading post founded by Greek settlers from Massalia in the 3rd century BC to trade with local Ligurians. Louis XIV ordered the razing of the castle because he feared the resistance of the people of Nice. Since 1882, the city of Nice has managed the hill as a public park, transforming it into a green space with panoramic views over the Baie des Anges. Today, only ruins remain of the castle, but the park includes archaeological vestiges and a waterfall, making it a favored spot for both locals and tourists.
